title: How to Make a Budget When You Earn Less Than $1,000 a Month
description: A step-by-step budget for incomes under $1,000 a month: what to pay first, a worked example, and what to do when the numbers don't add up.

cover.alt: Coins and notes being sorted into four jars beside a notebook

keywords: low income budget zero-based budget small income
takeaways: Percent-based rules break on small incomes. Give every dollar a job instead, starting with housing, food, transport and utilities.
Budget from your lowest normal month, not your best one.
If essentials cost more than you earn, the fix is on the income or housing side. No amount of coffee-skipping closes that gap.
body:
Most budgeting advice has one quiet assumption baked into it: that there will be money left over once the bills are paid. When you are living on less than $1,000 a month, there often isn't. So the classic rules ("save 20%", "keep housing under 30%") start to feel like they were written for someone with a very different bank balance. They were.

Budgeting on a low income isn't really about percentages. It's about order: deciding what gets paid first, what waits, and spotting early when a month simply isn't going to work. This low-income budget does exactly that.

## Step 1: Find your real monthly number

Dig out the last three months and write down what actually landed in your account, or in your hand. Not your hourly rate. Not what you hope next month looks like. What really showed up.

If the amount changes month to month, **build the whole budget off the lowest of the three**. Anything you earn above that is extra, and you decide what it does when it arrives. Budgeting from a good month is the most common reason a budget fails by the 20th.

## Step 2: List what it costs to keep your life running

These are often called the four walls: the things that keep your life standing. They get paid before anything else, no exceptions:

1. **Housing**: your rent, or your share of it
2. **Food**: actual groceries, not takeaway and delivery
3. **Transport**: whatever gets you to work or class
4. **Utilities**: electricity, water, phone, internet

Pull the real figures from your bank statement or receipts. Don't guess. Guessing low here is exactly how the plan quietly falls apart.

## Step 3: Add the minimums you owe

Right after the four walls come the minimum payments on any debt. Missing these costs you late fees and a dented credit record, which makes everything else in life more expensive later. You are not trying to clear the debt yet. You are keeping it from growing teeth.

## Step 4: Give every remaining dollar a job

Take your income, subtract the four walls and the debt minimums. Whatever is left, even if it is only $60, gets split between three things:

- **A small buffer.** Even $20–$40 a month. This is the thing that stops a flat tyre from turning into a new debt. See [how to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/).
- **Irregular costs.** The stuff that isn't monthly but is definitely coming: a bus pass renewal, exam fees, a phone that will eventually give up.
- **Personal spending.** A real amount, written into the plan, with your name on it. A budget with zero fun money doesn't get followed. It gets abandoned by the second week.

Keep assigning until income minus everything equals zero. This is called a zero-based budget. It does not mean you spend everything. It means nothing is left unassigned.

## A worked example on $950 a month

| Where it goes | Amount | Share |
|---|---:|---:|
| Room in a shared flat | $400 | 42% |
| Groceries | $180 | 19% |
| Transport | $70 | 7% |
| Utilities (your share) | $50 | 5% |
| Phone and internet | $40 | 4% |
| Debt minimums | $60 | 6% |
| Buffer / emergency fund | $40 | 4% |
| Irregular costs | $50 | 5% |
| Personal | $60 | 6% |
| **Total** | **$950** | |

Notice that the essentials eat about 78% of the income here. The classic [50/30/20 rule](/blog/50-30-20-rule-explained/) would allow 50%. That gap is completely normal when you are figuring out how to budget on $1,000 a month. It is not a sign you are doing it wrong.

## What this looks like when a month goes sideways

Here is a made-up but very ordinary month, using the budget above.

Sam works part-time at a café and usually takes home $950. In the second week the manager cuts two of his shifts, and he can see the month is going to come in at about $870. That is $80 short.

Without a plan, this is the month the phone bill gets skipped or the credit card comes out for groceries. With the budget, Sam already knows the order. Rent, food, transport, utilities and the $60 debt minimum don't move. The $80 has to come from the three flexible lines, so he takes personal spending from $60 down to $20, irregular costs from $50 to $30, and the buffer from $40 to $20. That covers it exactly.

It is not a fun month. He cooks at home, skips a night out, and the buffer grows by $20 instead of $40. But nothing is paid late, nothing new is owed, and next month he goes back to the normal numbers. That is all a budget on a small income is really for: when money gets tight, you have already decided what gives and what doesn't.

## What to do when the numbers don't add up

Sometimes the four walls alone cost more than you earn. Skipping lattes will not fix that. Look at the big levers instead, in this order:

1. **Housing.** It is usually the biggest line by far. A flatmate, a smaller room, or a longer commute can move the budget by more than every other cut combined.
2. **Food.** A realistic grocery plan can take 15–25% off without you eating any worse. Here are [25 ways to save on groceries without coupons](/blog/save-money-on-groceries-without-coupons/).
3. **Income.** At some point the honest answer is that the income is simply too small for the costs. A few extra hours, or a [side hustle that costs nothing to start](/blog/side-hustles-for-students-zero-investment/), often does more than another round of cuts.
4. **Help you qualify for.** Student hardship funds, fee waivers, local food programmes and government support exist for exactly this situation. Using them isn't cheating. It's part of the plan.

## Keep it going with a ten-minute weekly check

A budget made once and never looked at again is a wish list. Pick one day a week, spend ten minutes, and answer three questions:

- What did I spend since last week?
- Which lines are running ahead of plan?
- What do I need to move to cover it?

Moving money between lines is not failing. It is the budget doing its job.

## Tools that are enough

Paper, the notes app on your phone, or a plain spreadsheet will all work fine. If you want one ready to go, use our [free budget template for Google Sheets and Excel](/blog/free-budget-template-google-sheets/). If you want an app, a few are free for the basics; see the [comparison of free budgeting apps](/blog/best-free-budgeting-apps/). The tool matters far less than the weekly check.

## The first month will be wrong

Almost everyone underestimates food and forgets at least one irregular cost in month one. That is expected. Treat the first month as a measurement, not a test. Fix the figures, and month two will be close. By month three you will actually know where your money goes, which is the point of the whole exercise.
